title: Doing nothing, nothing undone
hook: the Tao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone (Tao Te Ching 37)

segments.voice: Yesterday, soft overcomes hard: the door that meets the frame gently and stays shut. Your line was soft overcomes hard. Did you lower your voice by one notch? Day one thousand ninety-nine.

Bread dough, under a towel on the counter. All afternoon, nobody touches it. Nobody kneads, nobody checks, nobody helps. And when the towel comes off, it has swelled over the rim of the bowl. This week's chapters kept circling that kind of thing: the army whose thorns outlast its win, the victor who mourns, streams finding the sea, the mirror turned back on yourself, the flood that claims nothing, the plain taste, the soft door. Chapter thirty-seven gathers it into one sentence, and today's word is the first half of it.
screen: `DOUGH UNDER A TOWEL.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES IT. IT RISES.` → `A WEEK GATHERED INTO ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do." Look at Legge's parentheses. He's warning the reader: this isn't laziness. The Tao isn't asleep. It just doesn't do things for the sake of doing them, doesn't push, doesn't fuss. And somehow, nothing is left undone. Second, what follows. The chapter says if rulers could hold on to this, all things would transform by themselves. Not be transformed by a decree. Transform, on their own, the way dough rises. Third, when wanting stirs. The chapter admits that even in that quiet, desire starts to rise up again: the urge to step in, to improve, to manage. Its answer is to settle that urge with the nameless simplicity, the same uncarved plainness we met in chapter twenty-eight. Fourth, stillness. The chapter ends: without desire, there is stillness, and the world settles itself. Tradition treats this chapter as the close of the book's first part, the part about the Tao. Tomorrow the second part begins. In a household or an office, the opposite looks like the parent hovering over the homework, the manager rewriting every email, the gardener tugging seedlings to help them grow. Sometimes the useful thing is to set things up well and take your hands off. The bread doesn't need you watching it.
screen: `DOES NOTHING, AND NOTHING IS UNDONE.` · `THINGS TRANSFORM BY THEMSELVES.` · `SETTLE THE URGE WITH PLAINNESS.` · `STILLNESS, AND THE WORLD SETTLES.` · then, large: `NOTHING WHICH IT DOES NOT DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing happen by itself. Start with the breath. Don't do it. Let it happen. Notice that the in-breath comes without you calling it, and the out-breath leaves without you pushing it. Stay with that a while. Then think of one thing in your life you've been hovering over: a project, a person, a plan. Picture setting it down on the counter and putting a towel over it. Not abandoning it. Just letting it rise on its own for a while. The bell holds the time.
Doing nothing. The first half of chapter thirty-seven's sentence: the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and so there is nothing it does not do. Today's word.
Your line: nothing undone. Choose one thing today you'd usually micromanage, set it up well, and then keep your hands off it. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-seven's 'doing nothing' as not forcing: setting things up well, then letting them unfold without constant interference.
